13364: Only John mentions Roman soldiers (a speira, a cohort) at the arrest and the hearing before Annas. Annas had been high priest (AD 6-15) and five of his sons and his son-in-law Caiaphas held the office after him; he remained the power behind the office. The Beloved Disciple is described as 'known to the high priest' (John 18:15), which Bauckham uses to argue he was a Jerusalem disciple. Pontius Pilate governed Judea AD 26-36; an inscription bearing his name was found at Caesarea Maritima in 1961.
13365: Entering a Gentile's house could be thought to cause ritual impurity, which would prevent eating the Passover meal; the accusers stay outside, and Pilate moves in and out. The Roman governor alone had the power to execute (John 18:31), the 'right of the sword'. 'King of the Jews' was a political charge: claiming kingship without Rome's appointment was treason against Caesar. The custom of releasing a prisoner at Passover is attested only in the Gospels.
13366:
The 'I am' in the garden (John 18:5-6) carries the weight of the divine name; the arresting party falls back as people fell before God's glory (Ezek 1:28). Jesus is not a helpless victim: he goes out to meet them, protects his own ('of those you gave me I lost not one', John 18:9), and accepts 'the cup the Father has given' (compare Ps 75:8, Isa 51:17).

Jesus' kingship belongs to Israel's hope: the Messiah as king (Ps 2, 2 Sam 7:12-16). 'Not from this world' means its source is God, not that it is purely spiritual or irrelevant to earth. Jesus' testimony to 'truth' (emet: God's faithful reality) stands against Pilate's cynical power.
13367: Believers facing hostile authorities, Jewish or Roman, would see their Lord standing calmly before both, in control of his own destiny. Peter's denials, beside the courageous Beloved Disciple, would comfort and warn those who had themselves failed under pressure.
13368: Jesus refuses the sword. His kingdom confronts power not with violence but with testimony to truth. And even the leading apostle denies him — failure is not the end of the story (see chapter 21).
13369: David crosses the Kidron in betrayal and sorrow.
13371: Rulers conspire against the Lord's anointed king.
13372: The cup of the Lord's wrath.
13373: The Jewish people as a whole demanded Jesus' death and bear collective guilt.
13374: John shows a small group of temple leaders with their police, plus Roman soldiers and a Roman governor; the Catholic Church's Nostra Aetate (1965) and most churches reject collective Jewish guilt (Brown, Levine).
13375: Crucified king, Passover lamb, buried in a garden
13376: Pilate has Jesus flogged; soldiers mock him with a crown of thorns and a purple robe. Pilate presents him: 'Here is the man!' The chief priests cry 'Crucify!' and say 'We have no king but Caesar.' At noon on the day of preparation for Passover, Pilate hands him over. Jesus carries his own cross to Golgotha; the inscription 'Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews' is written in Hebrew, Latin and Greek. Soldiers divide his clothes and cast lots for his seamless tunic. Jesus entrusts his mother to the Beloved Disciple. He says 'I thirst', receives sour wine on hyssop, and says 'It is finished', and gives up his spirit. His legs are not broken; a soldier pierces his side, and blood and water flow out. Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus bury him with about 75 pounds of myrrh and aloes in a new tomb in a garden.
13377: John's timing is distinctive: Jesus is condemned around noon on the day of preparation (John 19:14), the time when Passover lambs began to be slaughtered in the temple. The narrator stresses eyewitness testimony to the blood and water: 'He who saw it has borne witness... so that you also may believe' (John 19:35). This may counter docetic ideas that Jesus only seemed to have a body. The chief priests' cry 'We have no king but Caesar' is ironic, since daily Jewish prayer confessed God alone as King.
13378:
Roman crucifixion was designed for maximum pain and public shame; it was reserved for slaves, rebels and the lowest classes. Victims were flogged first, carried the crossbeam, were often stripped, and could hang for days. The heel bone of a crucified man named Jehohanan, with an iron nail still in it, was found in a Jerusalem ossuary in 1968, confirming that nails were used and that a crucified man could receive a Jewish burial. Breaking legs (crurifragium) hastened death by suffocation; Deut 21:22-23 required bodies not to remain overnight, especially before a Sabbath and feast day.

Jewish burial for an honoured person involved spices and linen. 'A hundred litrai' (about 75 pounds) of spices is a royal quantity; Josephus describes lavish spices at Herod's funeral. A garden tomb belonged to the wealthy.
13379:
Jesus dies as the Passover lamb: hyssop was used to put the lamb's blood on the doorposts (Exod 12:22), and none of the lamb's bones were to be broken (Exod 12:46, Num 9:12). John the Baptist's 'Lamb of God' (John 1:29) is fulfilled. The piercing fulfils Zech 12:10, 'they will look on the one they have pierced', a passage about mourning in Jerusalem that leads to cleansing (Zech 13:1). The divided garments echo Ps 22:18, the psalm of the righteous sufferer.

The seamless tunic may recall the high priest's woven robe (Exod 28:32). Blood and water may point to the temple's sacrifice and the river of living water (Ezek 47:1, John 7:38). 'It is finished' (tetelestai) means accomplished: the work the Father gave is complete (John 17:4). And at the cross a new family is created: the mother of Jesus and the Beloved Disciple are given to each other as mother and son.
13380: Readers would see that the shameful cross was in fact the 'lifting up' of a king and the Passover of the world. Those who had been afraid would take heart from Joseph and Nicodemus, secret disciples who finally stepped forward at the most dangerous moment.
13381: The glory of God is seen in a crucified man who cares for his mother in his agony. In John the cross is not defeat but completion. It also forms a new family that crosses blood ties.
13382: No bone of the Passover lamb broken.
13383: Hyssop used for the lamb's blood.
13384: They divide my garments and cast lots.
13385: They will look on the one whom they pierced.
13386: For my thirst they gave me vinegar.
13387: 'We have no king but Caesar' shows the Jewish nation rejecting God and being rejected.
13388: The words are spoken by the chief priests (John 19:15), a small leadership group; John presents them as tragic irony, not a verdict on the Jewish people (Brown, Keener, Levine).
13389: The garden, the breath of life, and Thomas's confession
13390: Early on the first day of the week Mary Magdalene finds the stone removed and runs to Peter and the Beloved Disciple. They run to the tomb; the Beloved Disciple arrives first; Peter goes in and sees the linen cloths lying and the face-cloth rolled up separately. The Beloved Disciple 'saw and believed'. Mary stays weeping, sees two angels, then Jesus, whom she takes for the gardener — until he says 'Mary', and she answers 'Rabbouni!' He sends her to tell his 'brothers': 'I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.' That evening Jesus appears to the disciples behind locked doors, says 'Peace be with you', shows his wounds, sends them as the Father sent him, breathes on them and says, 'Receive the Holy Spirit.' Thomas, absent, refuses to believe without touching the wounds. A week later Jesus invites him, and Thomas confesses, 'My Lord and my God!' Jesus blesses those who have not seen and yet believe. John states his purpose: these things are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God, and have life in his name.
13391: Mary Magdalene is the first witness to the risen Jesus, and the Latin tradition later called her the 'apostle to the apostles' (Hippolytus and later writers). In the ancient world women's testimony was often given less weight in court, which many historians count as a reason the story was not invented. John 20:30-31 looks like the original ending of the Gospel; chapter 21 follows as an epilogue. There is a textual variant in 20:31: 'that you may come to believe' (aorist) or 'that you may continue to believe' (present); the manuscripts are divided, and scholars debate whether the book is mainly evangelistic or for strengthening believers.
13392: The 'first day of the week' is Sunday, the day after the Sabbath. Tombs were often in gardens or orchards, so a gardener would be a natural person to meet. 'Rabbouni' is an Aramaic form of 'my teacher', and the narrator translates it for Greek-speaking readers. 'Peace be with you' (shalom aleichem) was the ordinary Jewish greeting, but now filled with new meaning after the cross.
13393:
The garden setting recalls Eden; the risen Jesus is mistaken for the gardener, the role of the first Adam (Gen 2:15). When he breathes on the disciples, John uses the same rare verb (emphysaō) as the Greek translation of Gen 2:7, where God breathed life into Adam, and Ezek 37:9, where the Spirit breathes on the dry bones. This is new creation: a new humanity and a restored Israel.

'My Father and your Father, my God and your God' (John 20:17) echoes Ruth's covenant pledge, 'your people shall be my people, and your God my God' (Ruth 1:16): the disciples are now Jesus' 'brothers' in God's family. Thomas's 'My Lord and my God' answers the prologue's 'the Word was God' and applies to Jesus the language Israel used for its God (Ps 35:23).
13394: Readers who had never seen Jesus would hear themselves blessed in John 20:29. Thomas gives permission to doubt honestly. The purpose statement tells them directly why the book exists: for their ongoing trust and their life.
13395: Jesus meets people personally — calling Mary by name, inviting Thomas to touch. Resurrection is the start of a new creation, and the Spirit is given for mission: 'as the Father has sent me, so I send you.'
13396: God breathes the breath of life into Adam.
13397: Breath enters the slain and they live.
13398: Seeking the one my soul loves and finding him.
13400: 'My God and my Lord' addressed to Israel's God.
13401: Breakfast by the sea and Peter restored
13402: By the Sea of Tiberias (Galilee), seven disciples fish all night and catch nothing. At dawn a stranger on the shore tells them to cast the net on the right side; they haul in 153 large fish and the net does not tear. The Beloved Disciple says, 'It is the Lord!' Peter jumps into the sea. Jesus has a charcoal fire with fish and bread and invites them to breakfast. Afterward he asks Peter three times, 'Do you love me?' and three times commissions him: 'Feed my lambs; tend my sheep; feed my sheep.' He foretells that Peter will die by being bound and led where he does not want to go. Peter asks about the Beloved Disciple; Jesus says, 'If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you? Follow me.' The narrator corrects a rumour that this disciple would not die, and the community affirms: 'We know that his testimony is true.'
13403: Most scholars see chapter 21 as an epilogue added after 20:31, possibly by the same author or by the community after the Beloved Disciple's death; Bauckham argues it was planned by the author as a balancing epilogue to the prologue. The correction of the rumour (John 21:23) suggests the Beloved Disciple had died or was very old, which troubled those who expected him to live until Jesus returned. Peter's death, foretold here, is traditionally placed in Rome under Nero, around AD 64-67 (1 Clement 5, a source outside the canon).
13404: Fishing on the Sea of Galilee was usually done at night with drag nets or casting nets. Peter, stripped for work, puts on his outer garment before jumping in — perhaps out of respect, to greet his master properly. A charcoal fire (anthrakia) is mentioned only twice in the New Testament: the fire where Peter denied Jesus (John 18:18) and this one. A shared meal in the ancient world was an act of reconciliation and restored relationship.
13405:
Peter's threefold denial is answered by a threefold restoration, and his commission is in shepherding language: God's people as a flock entrusted to faithful leaders, in contrast to the bad shepherds of Ezekiel 34 and in line with the shepherd of John 10. Jesus feeding the disciples with bread and fish recalls the feeding in John 6 and God providing for his people in the wilderness.

The 153 fish have produced many symbolic interpretations (Jerome said Greek zoologists counted 153 species of fish, suggesting all nations; others note 153 is the 'triangular number' of 17, or link it to Ezek 47:10, where fishermen spread nets from En-gedi to En-eglaim beside the life-giving river). Many scholars think it may simply be an eyewitness memory, while the unbroken net suggests a mission that gathers without breaking.
13406: For a community grieving its founding witness and perhaps uncertain about its relation to the wider church led by Peter's memory, the chapter honours both: Peter as shepherd, the Beloved Disciple as witness. Each disciple has his own calling: 'What is that to you? Follow me.'
13407: Failure is not final. Jesus restores Peter not with a lecture but with breakfast and the question 'Do you love me?' Leadership flows from love and means feeding others. And comparing callings is pointless; each disciple must simply follow.
13408: Fishermen with many fish beside the river of life.
13409: Shepherds who fail to feed the flock.
13410: God sends many fishermen to gather his people.
13411: A table prepared, a restored guest.
13412: The two Greek words for love (agapaō and phileō) prove that Peter could only offer an inferior 'friendship' love.
13413: John uses the two verbs interchangeably elsewhere (e.g. both for the Father's love of the Son, John 3:35 and John 5:20); most scholars (Carson, Keener, Brown) see stylistic variation. The point is the threefold restoration.
13414: 'The Jews' as the whole Jewish people
13415: Many readers, hearing phrases like 'the Jews sought to kill him' (John 5:18), take John to be describing the Jewish people as a whole as Jesus' enemies. In older Christian preaching this fed the charge that 'the Jews killed Christ'.
13416: Ioudaioi in John has several senses: Judeans, the Jewish people generally, and most often the temple-based authorities in Jerusalem. The same Gospel says 'salvation is from the Jews' (John 4:22), says many Jews believed (John 11:45, John 12:11), and has Jewish characters on both sides. Jesus, his family and disciples are all Jews; the very people afraid 'of the Jews' are Jews themselves (John 7:13). Scholars such as Raymond Brown, Craig Keener and Amy-Jill Levine stress this. Adele Reinhartz, a Jewish New Testament scholar, goes further: she argues that even read carefully John's rhetoric distances believers from 'the Jews' and has an anti-Jewish effect, and that honesty requires admitting this rather than explaining it away.
13417: Evangelical commentators such as D. A. Carson and Andreas Köstenberger fully reject antisemitic use of John and agree 'the Jews' usually means the leaders who opposed Jesus. Some add that 'the Jews' can also stand for the unbelieving 'world' as a theological category, and that John's strong words are a prophetic, intra-Jewish critique like those in Isaiah or Jeremiah, not ethnic hatred. Some translations now render it 'the Judeans' or 'the Jewish leaders' where context supports it, though others warn that this can hide a real difficulty.
13418: John was quoted in sermons, passion plays and propaganda that led to violence against Jewish people. Reading Ioudaioi carefully is a matter of truth and of love of neighbour.
13420: John 3:16 is often presented on its own as the whole gospel in one verse: God loves you, believe in Jesus, and you will go to heaven when you die.
13421: John 3:16 is the climax of a sentence that begins in John 3:14: 'as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up'. In Num 21:4-9 dying Israelites looked at the bronze serpent and lived. 'So' (houtōs) in 3:16 mainly means 'in this way': God loved the world in this manner, by giving his Son to be lifted up on the cross. 'Eternal life' is the life of the age to come, starting now. 'The world' in John is humanity alienated from God, which makes the love more surprising. Scholars such as Craig Keener and Marianne Meye Thompson stress the Numbers background.
13422: Evangelical scholars (Carson, Köstenberger) agree on the Numbers background and the meaning 'in this way', and would say the popular use is not wrong but thin: God's love, the gift of the Son, and life through trust are all in the verse. They also point out that John does speak of future resurrection (John 5:28-29, John 6:40), so the 'after death' hope is real, not a mistake.
13423: Reconnecting 3:16 to the cross and to Israel's wilderness story keeps the love of God from becoming sentimental: it is costly, cross-shaped love that heals the deadly bite of sin.
13424: 'Born again' as a one-time decision formula
13425: 'You must be born again' (John 3:3) is often understood as a moment of personal decision, praying a prayer to receive Christ, after which one is a 'born-again Christian'.
13426: Anōthen means both 'again' and 'from above'; Nicodemus hears 'again', but Jesus means 'from above' — a birth God causes by the Spirit (John 1:13). The background is Ezekiel's promise of water and Spirit to renew Israel (Ezek 36:25-27) and the valley of dry bones (Ezek 37). It is about God creating a renewed people, not a human technique. And Nicodemus himself does not 'decide' in one scene; he reappears gradually (John 7:50-51, John 19:39). Keener, Thompson and Brown emphasise the Ezekiel background.
13427: Evangelical scholars agree new birth is God's work, not a formula, and Reformed theologians in particular insist regeneration precedes faith. Many would still say the new birth is a real beginning that becomes visible in a moment of turning, and that conversion experiences are a legitimate way people come into the new life. The problem is not the idea of a beginning but treating a prayer as the cause rather than the Spirit.
13428: New birth as God's re-creation of a people keeps the focus on the Spirit's ongoing work and on a life of trust, rather than on a past event as a ticket.
13430: From the King James 'In my Father's house are many mansions', many picture individual luxury homes in heaven that Jesus is building for believers to enjoy after death.
13431: 'Mansions' is from Latin mansiones, 'dwelling places' or 'rooms'. 'My Father's house' in John 2:16 is the temple, and the image may be of rooms in the temple or in a large family house. The same word monē returns in John 14:23 where the Father and Son come and make their 'dwelling' with the believer now. The promise is about belonging in God's household, at home with the Father, rather than real estate. Some scholars (e.g. Mary Coloe) connect it to the temple; others note Jewish wedding customs of a groom preparing rooms, though that link is uncertain.
13432: Carson and others agree 'mansions' is a mistranslation in modern English, but maintain that 14:2-3 does refer to Jesus' future return and believers being with him, so a future hope is truly in view. The best reading holds both: dwelling with God now by the Spirit (14:23) and fully at his coming.
13433: The promise is not a better house but a closer relationship: the Father's home is wherever he is with his children.
13435: 'You are of your father the devil' has been quoted for centuries as if Jesus were saying Jews as a people are children of the devil.
13436: In context Jesus is speaking to 'the Jews who had believed in him' (John 8:31) and who now want to kill him (John 8:40). The point is moral parentage: whoever seeks murder and lies shows whose family they belong to, the same logic used by Jewish prophets and by the Dead Sea Scrolls (which speak of 'sons of light' and 'sons of darkness' inside Israel). 1 John 3:8-10 applies the same test to anyone who claims to be a Christian. Brown, Keener and Levine all stress that this is polemic within the Jewish family. Reinhartz warns that, however it began, its effect on later readers was devastating.
13437: Evangelical scholars agree it cannot be applied to Jews as a people and condemn its antisemitic use. They read it as a spiritual diagnosis that applies to all who reject truth, Gentile or Jew, and note that the same chapter has Jesus say 'Abraham rejoiced to see my day' — he does not reject Abraham's family but claims to be its fulfilment.
13438: This verse was used in medieval and Nazi propaganda. Reading it in its setting is a basic act of justice.
13439: John 14:6 and the question of other religions
13440: 'No one comes to the Father except through me' is often used as a proof text that all people of other faiths are excluded from salvation, sometimes in a combative way.
13441: Jesus says this to his own frightened disciples on the night before his death, in answer to Thomas's 'we do not know the way'. In Jewish idiom 'the way' (derek) is how one walks with God (Ps 119:30), and 'truth' (emet) is covenant faithfulness. Jesus is saying he is the path to the Father's home of 14:2: in knowing him they know the Father (John 14:7-9). It is a statement of comfort and identity, not originally an argument with other religions. Scholars differ on what follows for people who never hear of Jesus.
13442: Evangelical scholars (Carson, Köstenberger) maintain the verse really is exclusive: there is no access to the Father apart from Jesus, and that is consistent with Acts 4:12. Inclusivist evangelicals (e.g. Clark Pinnock) agree Jesus is the only way but argue he may save some who do not know his name. Both sides agree the verse should be spoken with the tenderness of its setting, not as a weapon.
13443: The verse's original tone matters: it is an invitation to know God as Father through Jesus, said by a man about to die for his friends.
13445: Readers divide: some read 'born of water and the Spirit' as baptism, others as physical birth (amniotic water) followed by spiritual birth.
13446: Jesus rebukes Nicodemus as 'the teacher of Israel' for not understanding (John 3:10), which suggests the answer lies in Israel's scriptures: Ezek 36:25-27 joins clean water and a new spirit as God's cleansing and renewal of his people. 'Water and Spirit' then likely describes one birth: cleansing and renewal by God. Many scholars (Carson, Keener) favour this; Catholic, Orthodox and many Protestant readers also see a reference to baptism, as did the early church. The physical-birth reading has fewer defenders among scholars.
13447: Sacramental traditions argue that John's readers knew Christian baptism and would hear it here, especially since John 3:22 mentions baptising. Evangelicals who read Ezekiel can agree that baptism later expresses this cleansing without being its cause. This is a genuine scholarly disagreement, not just a popular error.
13448: Knowing the Ezekiel background shows that new birth is God's promised renewal of Israel now opened to all.
13449: 'Eternal life' as only life after death
13450: 'Eternal life' is often heard as endless existence in heaven that begins at death.
13451: In Jewish thought the two ages were 'this age' and 'the age to come' (Dan 12:2). Zōē aiōnios is the life of that coming age. John's distinctive point is that it starts now: whoever trusts 'has' eternal life and 'has passed from death to life' (John 5:24). Jesus defines it as knowing God (John 17:3) — a relationship. Thompson, Bauckham and Keener emphasise this.
13452: Evangelical scholars agree strongly with this 'already' emphasis and note that John also keeps a 'not yet' — resurrection on the last day (John 6:39-40). So the popular view is incomplete rather than wrong.
13453: If eternal life starts now, Christian life is about present friendship with God and love for others, not only waiting to leave the world.
13454: John as a 'Greek' or anti-Jewish Gospel
13455: Older scholarship and some popular teaching said John's Logos came from Greek philosophy and that John is the least Jewish Gospel, written for Gentiles to replace Judaism.
